issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
David is a 38-year-old high school history teacher who still tastes the blood from that November evening. He had stayed late for parent-teacher conferences, and by the time he reached the parking lot, the school was dark and the lot was nearly empty. Two men appeared from between the cars, one shouting something he could not understand over the roar of his own pulse. The yell-loud and sudden-became the entry point of the memory. When the memory returns now, it is not just a picture: he feels the cold pavement under his back, smells the exhaust, and without warning tastes the metallic salt of his own split lip. After the image faded, he often found himself thinking that the world had shown him its real face that night, and that nothing he did would ever make it look away. The taste arrives unbidden, often in the middle of third-period lectures, forcing him to stop mid-sentence and steady himself against the whiteboard.

That taste, and the full sensory reliving that comes with it, has reshaped how he moves through his days. He scans exits as soon as he enters any room-the faculty lounge, the gymnasium, the grocery store-and finds himself studying the faces of strangers for signs of threat. In crowded hallways between classes, students jostling past trigger the memory of being surrounded and pinned down; the taste surges into his mouth, and he has to remind himself he is not on the ground. Each time the hall narrowed around him like that, the thought followed with cold certainty: this is proof that danger is everywhere, that no place is truly safe. He has started driving alone to work, avoiding the carpool he used to enjoy, because the proximity of a colleague in the passenger seat makes it harder to shake the sense that he is trapped. Because the memory arrived so fully and so often, ordinary sounds began to feel like warnings: the thud of a car door, the scrape of a chair, the sharp click of a lock. A student dropping a textbook makes him flinch, and the loud noise carries him straight back to that shout in the parking lot.

What frightens David most is how much the world feels unfair. The police took a report but never followed up, and the men were never caught. He had always believed that schools were safe, that the system would protect him, and the silence afterward felt like a second betrayal. This sense of institutional failure and profound injustice loops back into the memory itself: the more he dwells on the unfairness of what happened, the more vividly the taste and the shouting return, as though proving that the event is unresolved and always will be. He tells his wife that the world is dangerous now, that any street, any hallway, any car could become the same trap. That belief drives him to scan every face he passes, and every face he scans seems to confirm the danger-a tight jaw, a direct stare, a hand in a pocket. Feeling this constantly on guard, day after day, was the strongest evidence he had that the world really was as dangerous as his worst thoughts told him. His threat monitoring makes him more sensitive to crowding and noise: he notices when a hallway feels too full, when a student laughs too loudly, and each noticing triggers another wave of memory and anger.

The cycle has cost him. His principal has mentioned that he seems distracted during staff meetings, and David knows he has snapped at a student for tapping a pencil. He stopped driving his colleague to school, offering vague excuses, and he can no longer watch action movies with his wife because the unexpected sounds make him jump. What finally brought him to a therapist was the taste itself-a recurring, unwanted sensory echo that he cannot explain to anyone. He wants to believe he can walk through a crowded school corridor again without feeling his heart race, and he is terrified that he cannot.

violations.explanation: No paragraph shows that triggers (e.g., crowded hallways, loud noises) directly cause or reinforce negative appraisals (e.g., world is unfair, dangerous).
No paragraph shows that intrusive memories directly cause or strengthen negative appraisals; instead, negative appraisals are shown to trigger memories.
No paragraph shows that the memory itself leads to an increase in triggers; rather, memory increases threat monitoring which in turn heightens sensitivity to triggers.
No paragraph shows that the sense of threat directly causes or reinforces negative appraisals; the vignette shows negative appraisals driving threat monitoring, not the reverse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that triggers (e.g., crowded hallways, loud noises) directly cause or reinforce negative appraisals (e.g., world is unfair, dangerous).
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that intrusive memories directly cause or strengthen negative appraisals; instead, negative appraisals are shown to trigger memories.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph shows that the memory itself leads to an increase in triggers; rather, memory increases threat monitoring which in turn heightens sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that the sense of threat directly causes or reinforces negative appraisals; the vignette shows negative appraisals driving threat monitoring, not the reverse.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
